title: The mobile visit for an independent hotel
metaTitle: The mobile visit for an independent hotel
excerpt: On a phone, the first screen still has to show the room and a way to check dates. Design that screen first. Do not shrink the desktop poster.
alt: A white modernist building with stacked cubic volumes and tall windows against a pale sky, a structure judged from the street in one glance.
caption: The building is readable from the pavement. A phone homepage should be too. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs on the first phone screen?
faqs.answer: A crop of the room that still shows the bed and a wall, one true sentence, and a date control. Do not open with a crest, a splash, or a newsletter. The traveler is usually comparing you with two other tabs, one thumb at a time.

faqs.question: How should the date control behave?
faqs.answer: It should be tall enough to tap and quick to respond. Keep arrival and departure visible, and show a closed-date message beside the fields rather than at the top of the page. Use the same labels as the desktop checker.

faqs.question: What is a fair speed check?
faqs.answer: Load the page cold on a normal connection and see whether the room appears before you want to leave. web.dev's good bar is largest contentful paint within 2.5 seconds, a response to a tap within 200 milliseconds, and layout shift of 0.1 or less. Reserve space for the hero so the button does not jump.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
An independent hotel mobile website is where most travelers will make the comparison. The first screen still has to show the room as it actually is and offer a way to check dates. Do not let the desktop composition decide the phone page. The phone is not a shrink of the poster. It is the poster.

Nielsen Norman Group's research on page time puts a hard edge on that first screen: people often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and the offer has to be clear inside the first 10 if you want any longer attention. web.dev's Core Web Vitals say what "clear" costs in engineering. Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds, Interaction to Next Paint at 200 milliseconds or less, and Cumulative Layout Shift at 0.1 or less. A phone on a street network is where those numbers become visible.

## The phone is the comparison

Assume the traveler is standing somewhere slightly distracted, with two other hotels in adjacent tabs, thumb already tired. They are not at a desk with your brand film in full width. They are trying to finish a decision before a train, or in bed the night before they would rather not keep looking.

Design for that posture first. The room and the dates have to fit in the opening view without a pinch and without a scroll that feels like a gamble. If the desktop team designed a full-viewport image with a centered sentence and a tiny arrow, the phone inherits a crop of sky and a sentence cut in half. Throw that composition out for the small screen. You may keep it on a wide window only if it still shows the room. Often it does not, and both layouts should change.

Read the first screen out loud from the phone, not from a laptop preview that you squint at. The words have to be large enough that a person does not zoom. Zooming is a sign the type was chosen on a monitor. Increase the size until the sentence about the room fits in two lines and remains a sentence.

The other two tabs are one gesture away. You do not get a second introduction. Anything that delays the room, including a splash, a cookie wall that covers the dates, or a newsletter sheet, spends the 10 seconds on your needs. Put consent and mailing lists where they do not cover the checker.

## The first screen, specified

A workable first screen on a phone has three parts, in this order. A photograph of the room, cropped so the bed and a wall are both visible. One sentence that names the room's limit or its true advantage. A date control, or a button that opens it without a page transition you did not need.

The photograph should be the same truth as the desktop lead, recomposed rather than randomly sliced. If the honest crop no longer contains the window, use a different frame from the shoot, one that was directed for a tall frame. Do not rely on the browser to invent the crop. Art direction is two crops, chosen on purpose.

The sentence should not be a slogan. "A standard double on the lane, quieter on the far wall" is a first screen. "Welcome to a new kind of stay" is a delay. You have room for very few words. Spend them on the fact that changes the comparison.

The control should be usable with a thumb at the bottom of the screen if you can place it there without covering the room entirely. A checker glued over the picture can work if the picture remains legible and the control does not jump. A checker that loads late and pushes the picture down is the layout shift web.dev asks you to avoid. Reserve the space. Then load the tool.

If the full checker is too tall, the first screen can hold arrival, departure, and a continue action, with guests on the next step. Do not hold an essay. Do not hold ten fields. The job is to start the dates, not to complete your CRM.

## What desktop layouts steal

Desktop layouts steal vertical room for atmosphere. A navigation bar that is a sculpture. A margin that looks like a gallery wall. A film that plays in a wide aspect. When those choices are simply narrowed, the phone gets the leftovers: a menu icon, a cropped chandelier, and the dates below the fold.

Decide the phone's first screen as its own layout. The wide version can add the approach picture, a longer caption, and a second room. It should not add a different promise. The sentence about the lane stays. The button words stay. You are art-directing two frames of one page, not writing two hotels.

Watch for content that exists only on the wide layout. A limit that appears beside the hero on desktop and disappears on the phone will be missed by the majority of visitors. If it matters, it goes in the phone's first or second screen. If it does not matter, remove it from both.

Hover is not a plan. Any detail that appears only when a pointer rests on a picture will never appear for a thumb. Put that detail in the caption or in the next sentence. WCAG's mobile coverage is the reminder that the phone is not an edge case. For this buyer it is the main case.

## The date control, under a thumb

The control has to be tappable. Small date fields designed as delicate lines fail on a phone, and they fail more often for people with less precise touch. Give the fields real height. Separate them from nearby links so a miss does not open the about page instead of the calendar.

The response has to be quick. Interaction to Next Paint at 200 milliseconds or less is the web.dev bar for a good experience. A date field that waits on a heavy script before it acknowledges a tap feels broken, and broken checkers send people to the other tab. Load what the checker needs. Delay the rest: chat, analytics you do not read, a map tile, a film.

Show errors in the place the thumb just was. "Those dates are closed" beside the fields, with the next open night if you know it. A toast at the top of the page is easy to miss while the keyboard is open. The keyboard itself should not hide the error. Scroll the message into view when it appears.

Keep the same labels as the desktop checker. Arrival and departure should not become "start your story" on the phone. Consistency is how a person who switches devices mid-search does not book the wrong night.

## Pictures, type, and jump

A tall hero that loads without reserved space will shove the checker off screen just as the guest tries to use it. That is ordinary cumulative layout shift, and it feels like the site moved the button. Set the image dimensions. Do not inject a banner above the hero after the fact. Do not let a promotional bar arrive from a third-party script and push the room down.

Type should not overlap the picture unless the picture was composed for that overlap and the contrast still holds in daylight on the sidewalk. A white sentence on a pale bed disappears outdoors. Put the sentence on a solid ground if you cannot guarantee the photograph. Clever type on photography is a studio pleasure and a street failure.

Do not autoplay a film on the phone. It spends data, it covers the room, and it often starts with the pool. Offer a still. Let a person who wants the film start it. Most will not, and they are right. They came to check dates.

Test with the operating system's text size increased one step. If the first screen collapses into overlapping lines, the layout is too fragile for the guests you want. Fix the layout. Do not ask people to stay at the default size.

## A pass on a real phone

Run the pass on a phone you did not design on, over a normal connection, not the studio's network. Load the page cold. Time is felt, not theorized: if the room arrives after you have already started to leave, you are outside the 2.5 second paint that web.dev describes as a good experience, or you are close enough that the third-party widgets will push you over on a worse day.

Complete a date check with a thumb only. No pinching. Note every moment you zoom, wait, or hit the wrong control. Each note is a change, not a debate about whether mobile "matters."

Then do the same pass for the room page, the rate page, and the contact path. A fast homepage that leads to a rate page with a desktop table the width of a spreadsheet still loses. The comparison often finishes on the rate page. Give that page a linear reading order: room, what is included, what is not, dates. A table that requires sideways scrolling is a desktop leftover. Stack it.

Ask one person who is not on the project to find the lane, or whichever limit you are proud of having disclosed, without help. If they cannot find it on the phone, it is not disclosed. Move it up.

## After the screen works, the odd question remains

A working first screen will not answer every stay. A late train, a mobility question, a dog, a buyout. Those need a contact path that says what happens next, without becoming a ten-field trap. [What the contact page should ask, and what it should refuse](/blog/a-contact-path-for-an-independent-hotel) is the next piece. Read it after the phone pass, because most of those messages will be typed on the same phone.

When you want the first screen built around the room and the dates rather than around a desktop poster, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The useful test is dull and fair: a thumb, a street, and a traveler who still has two other tabs open.
